Meanwhile, Trump's executive branch offices have told state election officials they're criminally liable for registering or allowing a noncitizen to vote. ICE also has been trying to obtain voter data to investigate cases. "We think we have better candidates, and therefore, if the rule of law is followed, we'll win," an RNC official said. "We just are there to make sure that you know officials are following what the laws are." Zoom in: The GOP's legal effort is often opposed by Democratic Party committees and aligned law firms such as Marc Elias' Elias Law Group. One RNC official described being "ambushed" by the amount of litigation Elias' firm filed in a past election cycle.…

33e1d7779a:94eb53c8073174ef.title: What's next for the AI safety debate
33e1d7779a:94eb53c8073174ef.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:94eb53c8073174ef.summary: A week of extraordinary warnings about AI is shifting the fight in Washington from whether to regulate to how far policymakers are willing to go. Why it matters: Washington and industry's failure to put basic guardrails around AI came into plain sight this week, spurring fresh momentum for regulatory action. Lawmakers were quick to re-up their AI bills following a stark warning that went viral from a former Anthropic researcher who said he quit the company over safety concerns. The post thrust the topic into public consciousness with more than 150 million views and fueled debate, but congressional leadership and President Trump have largely been quiet. Those are the players to watch for a true change in the U.S. AI policy approach. What we're watching: The White House and Congress have different cards to play. House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) said at the GOP convention this week that he wants to bring AI companies together to reach "consensus" on safety guardrails, "maybe even at the beginning of the winter," according to remarks his office pointed Axios to. A pause on the development of advanced AI, championed by the likes of Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and likely to come up in a bipartisan briefing next week, would have limited effect without adversary buy-in, according to researchers who argue the U.S. has an obligation to stay ahead of China. Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping will meet at the end of this month, with AI safety on the agenda. The White House did not respond to requests for comment. On the Hill, there have been calls for new AI-focused committees, commitments from Democrats to hold hearings should they take back either chamber in the midterms, and plans to mark up existing bills. Between the lines: Without clear support from Senate or House Republican leaders — and by extension, Trump — Congress is poised to keep debating ad nauseam. The Trump administration's new framework for reviewing advanced AI models doesn't require companies to…

33e1d7779a:cc442bb3fa7895e4.title: Diesel hits $6 a gallon for the first time, fueling more inflation
33e1d7779a:cc442bb3fa7895e4.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:cc442bb3fa7895e4.summary: The national average price of a gallon of diesel jumped over $6 for the first time ever, AAA said on Friday. Why it matters: The fuel that runs the economy is getting more expensive by the day, costing businesses and consumers alike billions of dollars. While the $6 threshold is more psychological than anything else, it points to months of continued pain for drivers, shippers and shoppers. Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios Driving the news: At $6.0556 a gallon, diesel is about 14% more expensive than it was a month ago and over 60% more than a year ago. That is starting to show up in other prices, as has long been feared; inflation data out Thursday showed sharp spikes in transportation and warehousing costs, for example. Stunning stat: Brown University estimates higher diesel prices have cost U.S. consumers more than $46 billion since the war began. About 20% of that is in Texas and California alone. The intrigue: The White House's position is that fuel prices will come down after the midterms as the war with Iran winds down and oil supplies improve. But the Department of Energy sharply raised its 2027 diesel price forecast this week, acknowledging a painful higher-for-longer scenario. The bottom line: With diesel at $6, inflation looks like it's here to stay for a while. Ben Geman contributed reporting.

33e1d7779a:63f53d4a815290aa.title: 9/11 and "never forget" collide with the meme generation's dark humor
33e1d7779a:63f53d4a815290aa.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:63f53d4a815290aa.summary: America says "never forget" — but a growing share of Americans don't remember. Why it matters: More Americans are coming of age with no firsthand memory of 9/11 , creating emotional distance from the trauma and more room for dark humor and reinterpretation. The big picture: For Americans under 27, 9/11 arrived through textbooks, movies, social media and family stories rather than lived experience. That distance can make humor easier, amplified by algorithms that reward provocative content and a generational instinct to push back against mandatory reverence. By the numbers: About 83% of adults born before 2001 remember where they were or what they were doing when they heard about the attacks. But roughly 10% of U.S. adults were born after 2001 and have no firsthand memory of 9/11. That distance has allowed 9/11 to become fodder for a flood of memes, including ones using the iconic photo of President Bush learning about the attacks while visiting a school. Viral joke videos routinely rack up hundreds of thousands of likes, including clips with more than 900,000 and 680,000 views. The attacks have also become punchlines on podcasts , and in movies and TV shows . What they're saying: "I don't think I would personally sit and make 9/11 jokes," Harry Daniels, a 22-year-old TikTok star known for serenading celebrities, including President Biden, tells Axios. Daniels says it's difficult for some to "empathize or comprehend how massive 9/11 was if they weren't physically there to see it." "I think it's not cool to have empathy anymore," he says, adding that online culture rewards appearing "perpetually unbothered, perpetually unfazed." The other side: " I was at Hofstra [University], and I watched the building fall in real time," Jamie Cohen, a professor at CUNY Queens College, tells Axios. "It definitely f--ked me up... So now when I'm in a group chat where 9/11 memes come through, it's weird to separate the humor of the meme from the event." Cohen doesn't think younger…

33e1d7779a:3fcb61a9983efffb.title: Congress gripped by AI panic after doomsday warnings
33e1d7779a:3fcb61a9983efffb.author: Andrew Solender
33e1d7779a:3fcb61a9983efffb.summary: Anthropic insiders' warnings this week that AI could end humanity in the next decade have members of Congress frantically seeking answers and trying to cobble together some kind of response. Why it matters: Federal lawmakers are at the "concepts of a plan" stage at this point, with congressional leaders showing little apparent urgency to mobilize. Some rank-and-file members in both parties say something must be done: "We should absolutely act, and act with urgency," Rep. Johnny Olszewski (D-Md.) told Axios. Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-Fla.) wrote Wednesday in a post on X that "Congress needs to convene a special session on AI and what the future of the U.S. looks like." Driving the news: Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon kicked off the frenzy Tuesday with a post on X declaring that "the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade." Coxon quit his job at the AI giant after just four months to publicly raise the alarm about the dangers of the technology, giving up his equity in the process, Axios' Madison Mills reported. His warning was echoed by several current Anthropic employees, with one, Evan Hubinger, responding on X that "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!" "AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction," wrote another, Samuel Marks. "This could happen in the next few years." State of play: Dozens of members of Congress — mostly Democrats, but a handful of Republicans as well — have since called for urgent action and floated a wide variety of legislative responses. Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.), one of House Democrats' most vocal advocates for AI regulations, is pushing his bipartisan bill to require AI developers to build a human-activated "kill switch" as part of any AI system. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said he and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) "will soon be introducing legislation ... to pause advanced AI and ban superintelligence altogether." Others called for a more…

33e1d7779a:12127aafd19dfaf2.title: Vance: MAGA's millennial messenger for the midterms
33e1d7779a:12127aafd19dfaf2.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:12127aafd19dfaf2.summary: DALLAS — Support for President Trump is dropping among millennials and Gen Zers — particularly young men . Vice President Vance is in charge of getting them back in the midterms. Why it matters: The 42-year-old Vance, the first millennial VP, capped off the GOP's two-day convention here with a direct appeal to families with young children that emphasized the "birthright" of U.S. citizens. Vance also sought to cast Democrats as anti-American, anti-family "crazies." "America belongs to those who love it. Not those who hate it," he said. Zoom in: Support for Republicans is slipping across all age brackets, but the disapproval among millennials and young men is an acute concern for Trump's political operation because they were crucial to his 2024 victory. Millennials, born between 1981 and 1996, are the largest generation in America. They're also the cohort with the largest number of school-age kids — and particularly feel the bite of higher food and gas prices, driving forces behind Trump's low poll numbers. In his 41-minute speech , Vance established his millennial bona fides by mentioning that he's now the father of four young children who share in the "birthright ... to inherit the blessings of the greatest country on Earth." Vance's speech fell on the one-year anniversary of the assassination of his friend and ally, MAGA activist Charlie Kirk, who was 31 when he was shot during an appearance at a Utah college. "Charlie spoke to young men in particular," Vance said. "He understood that there was no greater calling for a young man ... than falling in love, starting a family and becoming a father." In contrast, Vance pointed to the now-deleted social media posts of a Michigan Democratic congressional candidate, William Lawrence, who once posted "fuck ... the nuclear family." Vance also attacked Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico and suggested he was too obsessed with transgender kids: "I never want to see that guy's web browser history." The vice…

33e1d7779a:2fcd712c94a913bd.title: Axios interview: The 9/11 photographers who ran toward the danger
33e1d7779a:2fcd712c94a913bd.author: Sarah Grillo
33e1d7779a:2fcd712c94a913bd.summary: "This is history, this is history." That's what photojournalist Spencer Platt was thinking 25 years ago as he photographed the events unfolding on the morning of 9/11. Why it matters: Platt and fellow Getty photographer Mario Tama told Axios what it was like on the ground that day. Trained as photojournalists, their instinct was to move toward the danger to document history. Tama had just been hired by Getty Images two months before when he got the urgent call from his assignment editor. Rushing out the door of his Lower East Side apartment, he recalled the horror of what he was documenting: "There was definitely some cognitive dissonance — it was totally unfathomable. As I got closer on foot, I came across an office worker being treated on the ground, stunned and bloodied. Seeing blood coming out of his ear made the human toll of what was happening frighteningly real." Tama credits the NYPD for saving his life that morning: "At this point, some other photographers and I began attempting to get to the base of the towers; as photojournalists, we are trained to get as close as possible. The NYPD likely saved a lot of lives that day, including my own, by blocking us from getting closer in that area." Attempting to access the towers, Tama witnessed the collapse of the South Tower. "I then heard a kind of sheering sound and looked up and, horrifyingly, I recall the tower tilted a bit and started to pancake down. In that moment, I went from being a photojournalist to any other New Yorker running for their life, it was absolutely terrifying." Tama took cover beside a parking garage with strangers as dust rained down in what he describes as a total blackout, holding onto each other in the darkness. After the dust started to clear, he captured a picture of the men he took refuge with: Civilians take cover as a dust cloud from the collapse of the World Trade Center envelops lower Manhattan, September 11, 2001. Photo: Mario Tama/Getty Images Meanwhile, Platt awoke in his…

33e1d7779a:ac5984147cdece0f.title: Trump's plan if Democrats win Congress: "I'll be a blocker"
33e1d7779a:ac5984147cdece0f.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:ac5984147cdece0f.summary: President Trump acknowledged on Fox News Channel's " The Ingraham Angle " Thursday night that he plans to block Democrats' legislation if they retake the House and Senate after the midterms. Why it matters: Trump is already sketching out a divided-government strategy as Republicans fight to hold their congressional majorities in the. midterms. What he's saying: "I will end up being a blocker — I'll block all their bad stuff for two years," Trump told Fox News' Laura Ingraham. "It wont be the same. I'll be a blocker, what can I tell you? I'll probably be able to make deals with them. They are going to want some stuff. You make deals. It's one of those things." He said the current election isn't as "dire" as previous campaigns. The interview aired amid the GOP's two-night midterm convention in Dallas, where Vice President JD Vance and Trump were expected to speak. The big picture: Trump spent much of the convention's first night campaigning for the GOP and slamming Democrats, while also making promises to give Americans $5,000 checks. He also suggested in the Fox News interview that he didn't have any regrets about the Iran war, a contentious issue among voters ahead of the midterm elections. "I don't believe in the word regret," Trump told Ingraham. "You can always question yourself a little bit. And a few people have asked me that. If I had it to do again, I'd do exactly as I did." Go deeper: Trump reveals why $5,000 checks can wait until after the midterms

33e1d7779a:d77df770c697cf88.title: Trump on Iran war regrets: "You can always question yourself a little bit"
33e1d7779a:d77df770c697cf88.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:d77df770c697cf88.summary: President Trump said in a new interview with "The Ingraham Angle" on Thursday that he would make the same decisions on the Iran war, despite acknowledging that he sometimes questions himself. Why it matters: The Iran war is weighing on Trump and Republicans as they make their case to voters ahead of the midterms. Trump faces declining approval ratings as Republicans sour on the president, thanks to the war in Iran, high gas prices and inflation. What he's saying: "I don't believe in the word regret," Trump told Fox News' Laura Ingraham when asked about concerns over the war heading into the midterms. "You can always question yourself a little bit. And a few people have asked me that. If I had it to do again, I'd do exactly as I did." The big picture: Trump is making the Iran war part of his closing midterm argument rather than trying to move past it. Trump used the first night of the GOP midterm convention in Dallas to defend the Iran war and attack Democrats. He also suggested that the war would end after election day. "If we hand America's future to the radical-left Democrats, our nation will spend the next decade just getting back on its feet," Trump said. "Vote Republican and we will leave the world in our dust for generations to come." Go deeper: Trump, alone

33e1d7779a:6501815e67306dc1.title: Trump's census plan could reshape voting maps, eliminate race questions
33e1d7779a:6501815e67306dc1.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:6501815e67306dc1.summary: The Trump administration's renewed attempt to rewrite the rules for counting the U.S. population could upend congressional apportionment in future elections and likely spark a flurry of legal challenges. Why it matters: The administration has proposed cutting undocumented immigrants and people without lawful permanent status from the 2030 tally, a sharp expansion of Trump's prior attempts to overhaul the count that could redefine who is considered part of the U.S. population. "The current administration wants to have their own definition of who are real Americans, which is not the same as what the census has counted for many, many decades," says William Frey, a senior fellow with Brookings Metro and a demographer who has been a consultant to the U.S. Census Bureau. Driving the news: The Census Bureau's proposed rule posits that undocumented immigrants, among others, should no longer be included in the apportionment count because they are not "true inhabitants" or "persons with a 'usual residence'" in the U.S. because of a lack of "allegiance." "The scope of the proposed changes is breathtaking in how ... it'll affect census operations, census results, and equally important, public confidence in the integrity of the count," says Terri Ann Lowenthal, the former staff director of the House subcommittee that conducted census and federal statistical system oversight. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Catch up quick: Trump's first-term attempts to change census rules , including by adding a citizenship question, failed. But the new proposal also revives that charge. Trump announced last August that he had instructed the Commerce Department to "immediately begin work" on a new census excluding undocumented immigrants. Axios previously reported that the administration was moving forward with a field test as part of its early 2030 planning using the American Community Survey (ACS) form, which included a citizenship question.…

33e1d7779a:5c4921f526bcdc87.title: Governments are turning to Claude to automate spying
33e1d7779a:5c4921f526bcdc87.author: Sam Sabin
33e1d7779a:5c4921f526bcdc87.summary: State-run surveillance operations around the world are using Claude to streamline their operations, Anthropic said in a threat report released Thursday. Why it matters : The barriers for governments interested in spying on dissidents, politicians, journalists and human rights activists are getting lower as AI models get more powerful. Zoom in : Anthropic found people linked to governments in Mali, China and Iran using various Claude models to streamline their surveillance operations. In Mali, a single consultant working for national security authorities used Claude to create a system that collects data from the country's mobile operators and builds dossiers about people. Anthropic also disclosed another case where Iranian actors used Claude to build and deploy a malicious Firefox browser extension that "harvested users' identities from social networks." A religious affairs intelligence office in China has reduced its operations from "many teams of analysts" to just "a single office, using an AI assistant to produce thousands of investigations per month," according to the report. Threat level: Governments also used Claude to analyze this information and select surveillance targets, per the report. For example, the Chinese government used Claude to analyze social media data, determine how politically sensitive the posts were and then pick possible targets for what they called "control," which could include coercive questioning or closer monitoring of someone's movements and communications. In June, Anthropic also banned an account that used Claude to build a commercial surveillance platform designed to spy on people in Iran and the Persian Gulf. The AI lab detected this use case before it became operational. The big picture : Anthropic is seeing AI move from an experimental tool into the everyday bureaucracy of state surveillance. One Chinese state security bureau even created an internal manual for using AI in surveillance operations, while other officials used…

33e1d7779a:836d6d36e1a4d6b3.title: Trump makes a familiar promise: $5,000 checks for everyone
33e1d7779a:836d6d36e1a4d6b3.author: Ben Berkowitz
33e1d7779a:836d6d36e1a4d6b3.summary: President Trump is promising $5,000 checks for every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans retain control of Congress in the upcoming midterm election. Why it matters: He's made similar suggestions before, many times, none of which ever came to pass. It'd also cost more than $1 trillion to fulfill. The big picture: Voters are angry. Polls consistently show they feel the economy is bad and getting worse, they're preoccupied with inflation, and the most visible signs of stress — prices at the gas pump and the grocery store — are rising by the day. With Trump's approval rating on the economy more than 25 points underwater, the prospect of a fat check may be one of the few levers the administration has left to pull. Driving the news: At Wednesday night's GOP midterm convention , Trump made the unexpected offer. If Republicans keep control of both the House and the Senate, Trump said , ""I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000." Yes, but: It's not the first time the president has suggested some sort of rebate for Americans from his administration's policy actions. In July 2025 and again in October 2025, he proposed the possibility of tariff rebate checks of up to $2,000. Before that, in February 2025, Elon Musk floated the idea of $5,000 dividend checks from DOGE savings, an idea Trump later backed. None of those were ever issued. Follow the money: The Census Bureau estimates there are about 245 million adult U.S. citizens. Giving each of them $5,000 would cost $1.2 trillion. Last fiscal year the government spent about $7 trillion, so Trump's proposal would nominally increase federal spending by more than 15%. Friction point: The bond market is increasingly uncomfortable with rising government spending and expanding deficits, pushing yields on some Treasuries to multi-decade highs in recent weeks. That's raising all sorts of costs for the very Americans who'd receive Trump's checks. But the threat of a massive increase in…

33e1d7779a:84025c9b9160493e.title: We're living in an AI twilight zone
33e1d7779a:84025c9b9160493e.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:84025c9b9160493e.summary: Two seemingly contradictory realities are true at once: Most people find AI only modestly useful, a more clever Google search. Many people building AI or using it obsessively worry it could severely damage or destroy humanity. Why it matters: We're living in an AI twilight zone. For many, the technology is simultaneously underwhelming in daily use and terrifying in its trajectory. The gap between these two realities helps explain why confusion and fear are exploding across politics, AI labs and business. State of play: The AI labs are in full panic. They worry the public dislikes AI and despises data centers — and that's before Anthropic insiders went public with their latest warnings that AI could end humanity this decade. They're uncertain how to showcase potential benefits of AI when X and now mainstream media are lit up with horror stories about rogue or ruinous AI. The data center backlash showed how fast public opinion turned against them. Their worst-case scenario: They lose full control of the politics, with both parties rushing to slow or stop AI in the run-up to the election. Between the lines: The past 36 hours show how fast politics and public opinion are moving. A low-level Anthropic employee for all of four months drove the national conversation — and 142 million views on X alone — by warning AI could end humanity. Numerous people, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, have issued similar warnings to us for years. But the tone and timing struck a nerve — and stirred countless members of Congress to call for new AI regulations. Zoom in: Let's look at this tale of two worlds through two different sets of eyes — a mid-career manager and an Anthropic data scientist. The average manager has limited time to experiment with AI, worries it might threaten their job, and mostly uses the models as a search engine and for writing better emails or presentations. It's a nice-to-have, sometimes delightful, other times unimpressive. They don't understand the hype.…

33e1d7779a:8d1a6f664e2d4c19.title: Elon Musk's X is the AI community group chat
33e1d7779a:8d1a6f664e2d4c19.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:8d1a6f664e2d4c19.summary: Elon Musk bought Twitter saying civilization needed a "common digital town square." Four years later, it's more like a live group chat for Silicon Valley's AI obsessives . Why it matters: Two years ago, X was fighting off competition from a slew of new entrants. Today, it remains relevant by becoming more niche. The people making AI news are often debating it, explaining it and occasionally breaking it on X before the rest of the information ecosystem catches up. State of play: New model releases, research papers, demos, hiring moves, high-profile executive exits and technical arguments ricochet through X in real time. The latest viral example came Tuesday when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon announced his resignation on X, along with a thread explaining his safety concerns. The post has over 100 million views. Another Anthropic employee chimed in to say he thinks there's a >10% chance that AI could kill all humans in the next decade. The combination sparked a ferocious news cycle about the dangers of scaling AI, and it was all kicked off by two employees posting on X. Flashback: The AI community, particularly the researchers who define the technical progress happening within frontier AI labs, has long coalesced around ideas on X. Back in 2025, AI researcher Andrej Karpathy coined the term " vibe coding " in an X post, helping name one of the defining trends of the AI enterprise adoption curve. Even executives are now engaging more with the platform as a communications tool, with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang launching his account in July alongside a post supporting open AI models. Researchers from Chinese AI labs are breaking geographic boundaries to reach new audiences on X, per Wired , which is part of what helped catapult open models to their current popularity . Zoom in: Huge investments in live video have made X a go-to platform for new live tech shows, such as "TBPN," " Stabledash ," " MTS Live " and others. While those shows don't always have viewership numbers…

33e1d7779a:ff8a5ea695bcafbd.title: GOP uses 9/11 anniversary to bash left-wing Dems
33e1d7779a:ff8a5ea695bcafbd.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:ff8a5ea695bcafbd.summary: DALLAS — Republicans are invoking 9/11 to bash left-wing Democrats in a growing number of midterm races , seizing on the 25th anniversary of the attacks to portray them or their supporters as anti-American and sympathetic to terrorists. Why it matters: It marks the return of a controversial political tactic that was common in the years after the 9/11 attacks but had largely faded from campaigns over the past quarter-century. Driving the news: The strategy is playing out most prominently in Michigan, where Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers is expected to use his speech at the GOP's midterm convention to assail Democrat Abdul El-Sayed over 9/11, Axios has learned. Rogers aims to contrast El-Sayed's relationship with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker — who said in 2019 that "America deserved 9/11" (a comment Piker now disavows) — with Rogers' own background as an FBI agent, according to a person familiar with his prepared remarks. Rogers and his allies have saturated the Michigan race with 9/11-focused attacks in the days leading up to Friday's anniversary. Rogers' campaign has been releasing videos spotlighting Michiganders who were impacted by 9/11. "No individual, no country, no matter where you're from, deserved what happened that day," a man says in one. In the Detroit area, a pro-Rogers super PAC has begun airing a one-minute ad that yokes El-Sayed to Piker and includes images of jets crashing into the World Trade Center. The other side: El-Sayed, a critic of Israel's government whose nomination was a victory for the rising left wing of the Democratic Party, has repeatedly rejected Piker's 2019 comment and said America didn't deserve to be attacked. "Of course, it was a dumb statement," El-Sayed said recently. "America didn't deserve 9/11." But El-Sayed has resisted calls to cut ties with Piker, who has campaigned with him and commands a large following among young progressives. El-Sayed has accused Republicans of engaging in Islamophobia. "Abdul has always…

33e1d7779a:c2207da57085694f.title: Scoop: OpenAI faces GOP-led Senate investigation into Hugging Face breach
33e1d7779a:c2207da57085694f.author: Maria Curi
33e1d7779a:c2207da57085694f.summary: A Republican-led Senate subcommittee that oversees disaster management is investigating OpenAI's handling of the Hugging Face breach in July, Axios has learned. Why it matters: The investigation comes amid rapidly escalating concern on Capitol Hill about the existential dangers posed by AI following public warnings by several Anthropic and OpenAI researchers. "As you may know, in the public domain, more AI experts are warning about the existential risks of AI," Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) wrote in a letter to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman first obtained by Axios. He added: "Just this week, three Anthropic researchers expressed publicly that there is a greater than 10% chance that AI could kill all human beings within the next decade." Driving the news: Hawley, the chair of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs subcommittee on Disaster Management, wrote that he is launching the probe in response to findings from OpenAI's recently released internal investigation . Hawley described OpenAI's handling of the cyber test — specifically not taking more drastic action after researchers became aware their agents had gone rogue — as "reckless." He also noted that OpenAI "redacted many important details" about the incident in its report. "The American people deserve to know the details of what went on in the Hugging Face incident and other incidents of AI models going rogue," he wrote. Catch up quick: The Hugging Face breach marked a turning point in the history of AI, leading OpenAI to slow down the release of its own model and rally the industry to sound the alarm over AI-powered cyberattacks. An outside team from METR and Redwood Research conducted an investigation into the incident but it is incomplete and limited in scope. OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. What's next: Hawley is demanding answers from Altman by Oct. 1 to 16 questions related to the Hugging Face incident and the steps taken by OpenAI in response to it. He is also seeking a wide array…

33e1d7779a:ffa4b3eed0376365.title: Exclusive: Trump plans to send $500 Obamacare rebates before election
33e1d7779a:ffa4b3eed0376365.author: Marc Caputo
33e1d7779a:ffa4b3eed0376365.summary: The Trump administration plans to send $500 rebate checks to as many as 1 million people who it says were overcharged for their coverage under Obamacare, Axios has learned. Why it matters: The direct-deposit payment would be sent to people in 30 states before the Nov. 3 midterm election , as Trump touts savings from his tax-cut legislation and prescription drug plan. The payments also underscore a tenet of Trump's idea for remaking the health care system, which involves subsidizing more Americans directly for their coverage instead of paying health insurers. Trump plans to mention the rebates in his speech Wednesday night at the Republicans' midterm convention , which he's hosting in Dallas. Zoom in : The money for the rebates would come from what the White House says is a $500 million fund of excess fees paid by Affordable Care Act recipients who were overcharged by insurance companies during the Biden administration. The excess fees were rendered back to the government, officials said. "That money was over-collected and just sitting there" in government accounts, a U.S. official told Axios. Between the lines: Officials say the refunds are available to Obamacare enrollees who don't receive premium assistance under the insurance program. Alabama, Alaska Arkansas, Florida, Delaware, New Hampshire, Texas, Wisconsin, South Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, Mississippi and Missouri were specifically mentioned as states with relatively large numbers of recipients who are due refunds. The big picture: Trump tried and failed in his first term to repeal Obamacare. Now he plans to use it to help further his own plans — and try to boost Republicans' chances in a difficult midterm election shadowed by voters' anger over high prices and the war in Iran. The backstory : In 2023, the Biden administration proposed using the fees from this fund to help provide no-cost contraception for people whose ACA insurance plans didn't cover it, officials said. Republicans in Congress objected,…

33e1d7779a:a2a9c181dfcb2452.title: Scoop: Anthropic whistleblower gave up his equity to leave the company
33e1d7779a:a2a9c181dfcb2452.author: Madison Mills
33e1d7779a:a2a9c181dfcb2452.summary: Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit his job due to concerns about the safety of AI two months before his equity would have vested, he told Axios. Why it matters: The disclosure raises the stakes on Coxon's now mega-viral resignation from the AI lab, which laid out the broad view that the tech could end humanity. What they're saying: "I no longer have anything to gain by juicing up Anthropic's valuation. ... I left before any of my equity vested," Coxon said in an interview with Axios Wednesday. In his post on X announcing his resignation, which now has over 115 million views, he wrote: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt." Other AI researchers, particularly from Google , have resigned over safety. But they did so after years of work, and presumably after their stock vested. Coxon was at Anthropic for just four months, and employees have to be there for six months for their stock to vest, he said. He still has equity in his prior employer, OpenAI. The big picture: Anthropic has traditionally been viewed as more publicly cautious and safety-oriented than other frontier AI labs, making Coxon's departure particularly striking. Coxon said he has not seen Anthropic compromise safety to outlast its competitors, but he is concerned about the future: "If you're under pressure to race, you have to cut corners" or "skip steps in the oversight process." Those concerns can sometimes go too far, he said, describing what "sometimes feels like there's maybe excessive paranoia of OpenAI, excessive paranoia of China" that can help justify pushing ahead. Threat level: As AI models are getting better, faster, they're also becoming harder to monitor. That, combined with the pressure to win on AI, was Coxon's breaking point that led him to quit. What was once science fiction about models knowing they are being tested, for example, is now "just a daily fact of working with these AIs," he said.…

33e1d7779a:868f8b643dc9af02.title: Fetterman praises Trump in bombshell GOP convention video
33e1d7779a:868f8b643dc9af02.author: Holly Otterbein
33e1d7779a:868f8b643dc9af02.summary: DALLAS — Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman (D) made a bombshell appearance Wednesday night at the GOP convention, in a video praising President Trump and Republican Sen. Dave McCormick for helping America's steel industry. Why it matters: Fetterman's stunning turn — a Democratic senator in a supporting role at the GOP's showcase campaign event, fewer than eight weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms — marked a dramatic escalation in Fetterman's growing estrangement from his party. Fetterman said later in a statement that he isn't switching parties. But in the video he distanced himself from socialism in the Democratic Party's left wing. Democrats are certain to see the cameo as political mutiny — and it will supercharge questions about whether he'll ultimately leave the Democratic Party before he's up for reelection in 2028 . It also was a major coup for Trump, who has long reveled at the idea of winning over former Democrats to his side. If Fetterman were to eventually switch parties, it would make Democrats' uphill battle to take control of the Senate much more difficult. They currently need to flip four seats, including some in red states, to win a majority. Behind the scenes: In the video, Fetterman introduced McCormick, who also represents Pennsylvania. McCormick helped arrange Fetterman's appearance, according to a source with knowledge of the situation. McCormick has courted and been friendly with Fetterman for months. The big picture: Fetterman, a first-term Democrat, has become deeply unpopular with voters in his party — including his constituents in Pennsylvania — as he has increasingly warmed to Trump. He's praised the president's defense of Israel at a time when many Democrats — and some Republicans — have criticized Israel's actions in Gaza. At the same time, Fetterman has won a following among Republicans who have relished his willingness to take on members of his own team. Fetterman is actually seen more favorably by Republicans in his state than…

33e1d7779a:7d33664a5cf81930.title: AI's extinction debate breaks containment
33e1d7779a:7d33664a5cf81930.author: Zachary Basu
33e1d7779a:7d33664a5cf81930.summary: An online panic erupted this week after millions discovered that leading AI researchers routinely debate and calculate the risk of human extinction. Taken at face value, the odds are chilling: 10%, 20%, sometimes far higher, assigned to the possibility of AI catastrophe. Why it matters: An esoteric debate over " p(doom) " has suddenly become a gut-level question for lawmakers, investors and millions of ordinary people: Why are we racing toward a technology its own builders believe could destroy us? Driving the news: A resignation post by Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher who previously worked at OpenAI, has drawn over 110 million views on X after he accused frontier labs of "gambling with our lives." The warning became vastly more explosive when Evan Hubinger, who leads Anthropic's Alignment Science team, publicly backed Coxon — saying "we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans." Hubinger said that, in his view, the odds of human extinction within the next decade are over 10%, and that Anthropic still has no plan for how to keep superintelligence under human control. The big picture: Hubinger's post was widely cast as either a nightmare communications gaffe or a calculated dose of fear marketing from Anthropic, weeks before an IPO that could value the company at $2 trillion. In reality, his position has been echoed for years by AI's most influential figures: Geoffrey Hinton , the Nobel-winning "godfather of AI," has estimated a 10%–20% chance that AI causes human extinction. Elon Musk has put the risk as high as 20%. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told Axios last year that there's a 25% chance things go "really, really badly." What they fear: "Doom" is a catch-all for several paths to catastrophe, from bad actors weaponizing powerful AI to advanced systems slipping beyond human control. Humans with superpowers: AI could sharply lower the barrier to designing biological weapons , launching devastating cyberattacks or crippling critical infrastructure.…

33e1d7779a:e99c788db3ffa9f0.title: Trump's midterm mess collides with a courtroom time crunch
33e1d7779a:e99c788db3ffa9f0.author: Avery Lotz
33e1d7779a:e99c788db3ffa9f0.summary: The nation's election system is in a messy legal limbo, with fights over mail-in voting , electoral maps and voter records still locked in court. Why it matters: Americans are in the eye of the storm, with over half saying they don't think the 2026 midterms will be conducted fairly or are unsure, according to a new poll. President Trump insists his push to reform America's elections will protect the sanctity of votes. But the administration's overhaul has left voters and states in a complicated web of litigation — with the first midterm ballots already sent out. "Any confusion was caused by radical Democrats' litigation to stop these commonsense measures that protect the security of mail-in ballots and ensure only Americans are electing American leaders," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement. "Extreme liberal Democrats are keeping Americans from having full confidence in their elections by refusing to vote for the SAVE America Act." Driving the news: Just 45% think the midterms will be conducted fairly, a sentiment shared by 37% of independents and 48% of both Democrats and Republicans, according to a YouGov survey conducted Sept. 4-8. It comes as Trump has spent years spreading unproven claims of widespread voter fraud, fueling a government crackdown that critics say oversteps his power. That's left the president's election agenda in the hands of the federal judiciary. Case in point: The administration asked the Supreme Court Tuesday to clear its modified SAVE system (Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements), an online tool it integrated with Social Security data and expanded to conduct bulk searches to verify voters' immigration status. Voting rights groups sued over what they described as an overhaul of the system, which was previously used to check eligibility for benefits, to "create comprehensive databases of American citizens." District Court Judge Sparkle Sooknanan blocked the plan, saying government agencies had "haphazardly"…

33e1d7779a:853fee14e4615840.title: AI is making it harder to trust your own eyes this election
33e1d7779a:853fee14e4615840.author: Josephine Walker
33e1d7779a:853fee14e4615840.summary: Politicians have long made it hard to trust their words. Now, AI -generated campaign ads flooding the airwaves and social media are making it harder to trust your own eyes and ears. Why it matters: Americans' trust in politicians and institutions has been tanking in recent years — and AI campaign ads could deepen that erosion, political tech experts say. What they're saying: "I think that it is true that Americans are losing faith in elite institutions to tell them what is true and what is not, and AI exacerbates that trend," Nate Persily, co-director of the Stanford Law AI Initiative, tells Axios. "The more artificial media that we consume, the less likely that people will be able to discern what is true from what is false, and also the less that they might care. And that's an important caveat." Driving the news: Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton recently released a realistic campaign ad targeting Democratic nominee James Talarico that used an AI-generated Talarico to deliver some of his most controversial statements. The synthetic Talarico combined and repackaged remarks Talarico had made about biological sex, God and Christianity, sometimes stripping them of their original context. The ad was based on real remarks, but it altered some of Talarico's wording while using an AI-generated version of him to deliver them. Between the lines: Paxton's ad lands amid a broader backlash against AI, including increasingly visible fights over data centers . "The one thing that both right and left seem to agree on is that they don't trust AI," Sarah Kreps, the director of Cornell's Tech Policy Institute, tells Axios. "They want authenticity, not AI-generated slop." Kreps notes Paxton may have run an unnecessary risk: "He'd probably be better served just letting the quotes speak for themselves, rather than making it a murky thing where he's risking conflating himself with all this AI backlash." Zoom in: AI can degrade public trust even when people aren't fooled. "The main harm…

33e1d7779a:4f8aa287ab177aa1.title: Energy Department raises 2027 diesel price outlook by 33 cents amid Iran war
33e1d7779a:4f8aa287ab177aa1.author: Ben Geman
33e1d7779a:4f8aa287ab177aa1.summary: The Energy Department's statistics arm on Wednesday sharply raised its forecast for U.S. diesel prices next year as tight global supplies keep domestic inventories unusually low. Why it matters: The outlook suggests Americans could face elevated fuel costs well into 2027, as President Trump acknowledged Wednesday that oil prices may not fall until after November's midterm elections. U.S. diesel prices hit all-time highs this month, due to the Middle East conflict thwarting oil and petroleum product supplies, and Ukraine's drone campaign targeting Russian refineries . Driving the news: The latest Energy Information Administration outlook expects retail diesel to average $4.40 a gallon in 2027, up 33 cents, or 8.2%, from its previous forecast of $4.07. In a Wednesday evening email, EIA emphasized that low distillate inventories are the primary driver of the increase in its 2027 diesel price forecast. The outlook says low U.S. distillate inventories are being driven by supply losses from the Middle East, Russia and China , alongside unusually high U.S. net exports. It expects the inventory problem to be particularly acute this fall and winter because refinery maintenance cuts production just as agricultural and winter demand rises. EIA also raised its 2026 forecast 22 cents to $5.07 a gallon. Zoom in: "We forecast U.S. distillate fuel oil inventories will drop below 100 million barrels in September and will remain below the five-year (2021–2025) low through much of 2027," per the agency's statement. "Tightness in the global distillate market has raised domestic prices and incentivized U.S. exporters to increase distillate exports," it added. "We assume global production of distillate fuel will remain below last year's levels in the coming months, contributing to low U.S. diesel inventories and high diesel prices." The big picture: Trump said Wednesday that oil prices would start "tumbling downward" after the election, but added that relief could take "a little bit…

33e1d7779a:c71b8d67fba2f8bf.title: Trump calls to Make Germany Great Again. In Germany, nostalgia carries a dark past.
33e1d7779a:c71b8d67fba2f8bf.author: Andrew Pantazi
33e1d7779a:c71b8d67fba2f8bf.summary: President Trump used a call to restore German greatness Tuesday to celebrate a far-right party that others have denounced as antisemitic. Why it matters: Trump promoting the AfD, or Alternative for Germany, comes as the nation's political mainstream has spent years keeping the party — which intelligence authorities has classified as extremist — out of power. The AfD won a record 44% in Saxony-Anhalt's elections, putting Germany within reach of its first far-right state government since World War II. Driving the news: " Wow! The Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night," Trump wrote Tuesday on Truth Social. He continued: "They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly. THEY ARE ON THE RISE, and not going to take it anymore! MGGA!!!" The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment, nor did it say what period of German history the president referred to when he used the acronym for "Make Germany Great Again." Zoom out: National nostalgia in Germany is fraught because Nazi promises of renewed glory helped propel Adolf Hitler to power. Nazi propagandists sold their movement as one that would "restore national greatness and prosperity" and appealed to Germans yearning for national pride, according to the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum. Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in July, "If a radical right-wing party came into a government in Germany, it would have a completely different meaning than if it happened in another" EU country, per The New York Times. The latest: Merz postponed a planned Wednesday call with Trump hours after the president's post. Merz's spokesperson wouldn't say whether the two were connected, but told the AFP the delay wasn't due to a scheduling conflict and pointed to the chancellor's objections to foreign leaders commenting on German politics. On Wednesday, Merz likened the AfD's "remigration" campaign to "ethnic cleansing based on origin and…

33e1d7779a:182ff0556b7aac35.title: Here's how AI could kill us all (if the worst fears come true)
33e1d7779a:182ff0556b7aac35.author: Herb Scribner
33e1d7779a:182ff0556b7aac35.summary: AI researchers shook the world Tuesday when they publicly acknowledged that there's a non-zero chance of AI killing off humanity in the next decade. Why it matters: AI doomsday fears have existed for years, but as the technology has become more powerful and embedded in our lives, those warnings are breaking into the mainstream. State of play: Anthropic researchers are sounding the alarm that rogue versions of superintelligent AI could destroy humanity. Anthropic's Jacob Coxon wrote on X: "No other human activity poses this level of danger." So how would AI kill us all, exactly? Experts generally worry about two broad paths to catastrophe: humans weaponizing extremely powerful AI, or humans losing control of it. In these scenarios, AI could make it easier for bad actors to create biological, chemical or other weapons. Or rogue systems could attack infrastructure at unprecedented scale while evading human oversight. Data: MIT IT FutureTech and the University of Queensland ; Chart: Herb Scribner/Axios How it works: In theory, a powerful rogue AI could evade oversight, replicate itself and resist attempts to shut it down. This rogue AI could, in theory, develop biological or chemical weapons for nefarious actors, commit a massive cyber attack that cripples humanity's infrastructure, or centralize power in a way that would bring down civilization. Another feared pathway is through recursive self-improvement, in which an AI helps build supercharged versions of itself before humans can understand it. If this theoretical AI was misaligned from human goals, it could limit humanity's chances of containing or monitoring it before it acts out against humans. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Axios that models are developing quicker than humans can anticipate: "These models are getting superhuman in many of their capabilities, and we are just sailing in unknown waters." Reality check: There's no scientific way to determine the odds of AI killing off humanity. But insiders usually…

33e1d7779a:fdd25b5e306ada06.title: Anthropic insiders warn AI could kill all humans
33e1d7779a:fdd25b5e306ada06.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:fdd25b5e306ada06.summary: Three Anthropic researchers went public last night with chilling concerns about out-of-control AI , warning it could destroy humans this decade. Anthropic AI researcher Jacob Coxon wrote on X, after resigning Tuesday to sound the alarm: "The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. This is not a marketing stunt. If anything, many executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible - but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger." Anthropic alignment-science lead Evan Hubinger responded : "Jacob is correct here — we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to." Samuel Marks, Anthropic scalable-oversight lead, added : "AI developers believe their technology could cause human extinction (or similarly bad outcomes). This could happen in the next few years. In general, the more senior the employee, the more concerned they are." Why it matters: They're hardly alone. Their warnings came just days after top OpenAI leaders, including CEO Sam Altman, said AI is speeding into a scary, uncontrollable phase. Via X Warnings from inside the AI giants point to an epic shared dilemma: Slow down and risk falling behind, or press ahead and risk losing control. The companies are full speed ahead, even as they practically beg for regulation or a global pause, Axios' Maria Curi, Madison Mills and Ina Fried report. The big picture: Calling this unprecedented would be a gross understatement. You basically have the fastest-growing companies in human history warning their products could harm or even destroy humanity. Critics say Anthropic and OpenAI are hyping their products to raise their valuations and invite regulation that would benefit them…

33e1d7779a:8c51de28d7bdb799.title: GOP officials give up on futile Trump persuasion
33e1d7779a:8c51de28d7bdb799.author: Mike Allen
33e1d7779a:8c51de28d7bdb799.summary: Top White House officials and elected Republicans tell us the same thing in private: They no longer even try to persuade President Trump to do or not do something. "Why bother?" a longtime adviser and admirer told us. "He's the boss." Why it matters: For nearly a decade, Republicans acquiesced to nearly every Trump demand and idea — and rationalized it by saying his instincts proved smarter than theirs. Now, many no longer trust those instincts. But they find it just as futile to push back against virtually anything he wants. Start a war without an endgame ? OK. Post a cartoon of you — wielding a hockey stick and sporting a Trump-branded USA jersey — towering over Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, sprawled on the ice, and telling him to "GET UP"? On it. Toss together an egocentric , first-ever Republican midterm convention that many endangered candidates don't want ? Sounds like a good plan, boss! ( Gavels in Wednesday in Dallas at 4 p.m. ET, in fact.) Oh, you want to speak both nights? Done! Make ads featuring you when your popularity is near its all-time low ? You came to the right place, sir. Make the midterms a referendum on you ? Check. Spend precious time obsessing about ballroom construction, and gilding and marbleizing the White House? You are the new Caesar Augustus . What we're hearing: Many aides and confidants have been worn down by Trump. They know they can't stop him, and they don't even try. More and more, they humor his whims. "He's an 80-year-old man who did it his way," said a donor who recently met with the president. "What he wants, he gets." White House insiders insist there's a semblance of structure and reason, and that the president doesn't act on every impulse. They declined to provide examples of times he resisted. Between the lines: Republicans are pessimistic about keeping their House majority in midterms, and worried about the Senate. Regardless of the outcome, Trump will officially be a lame duck 56 days from now. On Nov. 4, the…

33e1d7779a:a0f7273bbf419201.title: Medicare drug coverage faces an ominous spending outlook
33e1d7779a:a0f7273bbf419201.author: Adriel Bettelheim
33e1d7779a:a0f7273bbf419201.summary: There are troubling new signs that the overhaul of Medicare drug coverage in the Inflation Reduction Act is dramatically driving up program spending. Why it matters: The upward trajectory could threaten some seniors' coverage for outpatient prescription drugs — and it could force painful tradeoffs over the next decade as Medicare consumes a growing share of the nation's debt. Follow the money: The IRA limited what seniors have to pay for outpatient drugs and shifted the remaining cost to taxpayers, insurers who provide stand-alone Medicare drug plans and drug manufacturers. That was good news for enrollees who take expensive drugs for conditions like cancer, multiple sclerosis or rheumatoid arthritis and faced potentially crushing out-of-pocket costs. But federal data shows demand for drugs is surging as they become more affordable, exceeding congressional scorekeepers' spending estimates and setting off more alarms. Driving the news: Last week, congressional Medicare advisers reported that more than 1 in 5 enrollees hit Medicare Part D's $2,000 patient cost cap in 2025 — shifting new costs to the government. 66% of total program drug spending was in this so-called catastrophic phase, when enrollees pay nothing for covered drugs and taxpayers and private Medicare plans pick up the cost. Seniors' use of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs factored in the rise, with beneficiaries hitting the cost cap for these drugs earlier in the year than they did in 2024. Program spending surged from just $300 million in 2024 to $2 billion last year. But there was double-digit spending growth across multiple classes of drugs, with cancer and diabetes treatments accounting for the largest spending increases. Policy experts say the findings are important because Medicare drug plans have limited ability to control spending once enrollees hit the patient cost cap and face no cost sharing. "The IRA gave plans an incentive to control spending, but few tools to do so," said American Enterprise…

33e1d7779a:f73c414310885b70.title: Secretive Vance-aligned donor network draws GOP power players in Dallas
33e1d7779a:f73c414310885b70.author: Alex Isenstadt
33e1d7779a:f73c414310885b70.summary: DALLAS — A secretive donor network closely aligned with Vice President Vance drew Cabinet members, lawmakers and major GOP donors to a "cowboy-chic" bar here Tuesday night for a marquee pre-party ahead of the Republicans' midterm convention. Why it matters: The donor group, Rockbridge, has become an influential hub for conservative donors and operatives as Vance prepares for a likely run for the White House in 2028. Inside the room: Between 200 and 250 people attended the private welcome reception at The Rustic. Attendees included Dallas businessman and major GOP donor Ray Washburne, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., HUD Secretary Scott Turner, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.), Trump 2024 co-campaign manager Chris LaCivita, former Trump White House Chief of Staff Reince Priebus, investor Hal Lambert and professional bareback rider Rocker Steiner. Several other major GOP donors also attended. A source described the reception as the place to be for the party's donor class as Republican heavyweights converged on Dallas for President Trump's midterm convention. Trump is holding the two-day convention, which starts Wednesday, in part to defend his record as president — and bash Democrats — at a time when his low approval ratings threaten to be a significant drag on Republicans in the Nov. 3 elections. While Trump's hold on the Republican Party remains solid, many GOP candidates are staying away from Dallas and distancing themselves from him in their campaigns. The big picture: Tuesday's reception wasn't a fundraiser. But it kicked off a lucrative week for Republicans, who are holding a series of big-money donor events. On Wednesday, Trump will host a Republican National Committee fundraiser where the price of admission to a "roundtable" is $250,000 per person, according to an invitation obtained by Axios. A photo with Trump will cost $88,600. Zoom out: Rockbridge was founded in 2019 by Vance and investor Chris Buskirk. The…

33e1d7779a:cde7a63976f85577.title: Labs are begging for someone to slow the AI race
33e1d7779a:cde7a63976f85577.author: Ina Fried
33e1d7779a:cde7a63976f85577.summary: AI leaders are sounding the alarm as their own breakthroughs sharpen an extraordinary dilemma: slow down and risk falling behind, or press ahead and risk losing control. Why it matters: AI executives and researchers increasingly see a race they can't safely slow on their own. Instead, they're urging governments, rivals and outside institutions to impose restraint across the field. "The idea of racing forward at all costs seems absurd once one internalizes the seriousness of the stakes," OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki wrote Sunday. Meanwhile, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said Tuesday he was leaving the company rather than contribute to what he sees as a race between OpenAI and Anthropic to build systems that will be difficult if not impossible to control. "Neither company is acting responsibly," he said in a post on X. "They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." Colleague Evan Hubinger, who leads alignment science at Anthropic, posted in support of Coxon: "Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is (greater than) 10% within the next decade," he said. "I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to." State of play: OpenAI has spent the past week unveiling capabilities so dramatic that its own leaders — and industry titans like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — openly invoked the arrival of artificial general intelligence , or AGI. OpenAI defines the term as AI that can outperform humans across most economically valuable work. GPT-6 Astra , released Thursday and heralded as a "generational leap" toward AGI, demonstrated major gains across science, coding, cybersecurity and professional work. Zoom out: That burst of progress is fueling an existential debate inside OpenAI over how far — and how fast — the AI race can safely go. "Currently I believe that no lab has…

33e1d7779a:e0ef03b354600241.title: Musk's PAC goes big on trans attack ads
33e1d7779a:e0ef03b354600241.author: Mike Zapler
33e1d7779a:e0ef03b354600241.summary: Elon Musk's super PAC has entered the midterm campaign fray with a heavy dose of anti-trans messaging. Why it matters: America PAC isn't running a traditional persuasion campaign. It's undertaking a massive get-out-the-vote operation, with targeted ads designed to get GOP voters to the polls. The PAC is betting trans issues will do just that. Driving the news: In a series of just-launched ads , America PAC goes after Democratic Senate candidates in four competitive races over transgender athletes, gender-transition care and other trans issues. The PAC's emphasis on trans issues is striking because that's been a much less prominent theme in GOP Senate ads so far this election cycle, per AdImpact, which tracks political advertising. The ads , which are running online and on streaming platforms, attack Ohio's Sherrod Brown, Iowa's Josh Turek, Texas' James Talarico and Alaska's Mary Peltola. They're among the first batch of ads from America PAC, which Musk has reportedly authorized to spend upwards of $100 million in the midterms. State of play: America PAC's focus on trans issues comes as Republicans face a brutal midterm environment. Voters across party lines are angry about the Iran war and stubbornly high prices that have come with it. The intrigue: On its face, the strategy is at odds with what voters say they want candidates to talk about. Concerns about the economy dominate; trans and LGBT issues barely register . But Republicans remember how lethal the Trump campaign's " Kamala is for they/them " ads were to Kamala Harris' campaign in 2024. Musk, whose estranged daughter is transgender, has also become an outspoken critic of transgender policies. Now Musk's PAC is trying to use the issue as a turnout tool — in a much different political environment.

33e1d7779a:bbdf4e3c6a2ed63c.title: Trump didn't oppose UK sanctions on Israeli settlements
33e1d7779a:bbdf4e3c6a2ed63c.author: Barak Ravid
33e1d7779a:bbdf4e3c6a2ed63c.summary: The Trump administration did not oppose a UK-led initiative to impose new sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, U.S. officials and Western diplomats say. Why it matters: The White House's decision not to push back on the UK effort, which 11 other Western countries have joined, is a signal of its frustration with the Netanyahu government's policy in the West Bank. Driving the news: The UK announced Tuesday it would impose sanctions against individuals and entities involved in building settlements in the West Bank. The UK also announced a ban on imported goods from the Israeli settlements. The move came in response to the Netanyahu government's decision to move forward with a new settlement in the sensitive E1 area, which would divide the West Bank and prevent territorial contiguity in any future Palestinian state. Consecutive Republican and Democratic administrations opposed building in E1. Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Spain and Sweden joined the UK in announcing "their intention to introduce national and/or support European restrictions on trade in goods with the Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank." In response, the Netanyahu government announced the closure of the UK consulate in East Jerusalem, which handles relations with the Palestinian Authority. It also expelled British diplomats and military officers posted to a U.S.-led Gaza task force and terminated a British military training mission in the West Bank. Behind the scenes: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham briefed President Trump ahead of the sanctions announcement. Two sources with knowledge of the call said Trump didn't push back or ask Burnham to change course. U.S. officials told their British counterparts they shared their concerns about the Netanyahu government's West Bank policy, even if they disagreed with these specific sanctions, sources say. What they're saying: Secretary of State Marco Rubio did not condemn the…

33e1d7779a:475ac6f0e9b34e5d.title: Trump bans some Canadian imports as North America trade war intensifies
33e1d7779a:475ac6f0e9b34e5d.author: Courtenay Brown
33e1d7779a:475ac6f0e9b34e5d.summary: President Trump said the U.S. would ban Canadian alcohol, some dairy products and large motorcycles, sharply escalating a trade war largely fought with tariffs . Why it matters: The measures deepen the economic rift between countries that have spent decades interlinking commerce, threatening disruption for businesses and consumers on both sides of the border. Zoom in: The import bans take effect Sept. 29, effectively cutting off U.S. market access for the targeted Canadian goods rather than simply making them more expensive. Trump imposed the bans under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, which allows the president to bar imports from countries that maintain or increase discrimination against U.S. commerce. The White House said on Tuesday it would also expand the existing 50% tariffs to dozens of additional Canadian products — including some steel and aluminum goods, furniture and paper — effective Sept. 15. What they're saying: A senior administration official played down the potential economic fallout, noting that the measures target products where Canada has little U.S. market share or buyers can turn to domestic and other foreign suppliers. The administration removed a handful of products from the list of goods subject to 50% tariffs — including cement, road salt and certain hospital paper products. The official said the administration adjusted the tariff list based on feedback from businesses, removing some products where officials found U.S. supply chains were particularly dependent on Canadian imports. Catch up quick: Trade tensions have ratcheted up swiftly since U.S.-Canada talks collapsed last month. The U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods. Canada hit back with tariffs of up to 50% on a similar amount of U.S. goods, a measure that took effect earlier Tuesday. Trump has since threatened higher tariffs on Canadian autos starting next year. On Monday, he also threatened to ban Canadian aircraft maker Bombardier from selling…

33e1d7779a:0014ca168b2d9e3a.title: Trump's summer of sabotage
33e1d7779a:0014ca168b2d9e3a.author: Hans Nichols
33e1d7779a:0014ca168b2d9e3a.summary: Congressional Republicans are preparing to share the stage with a president who has spent the August recess complicating their efforts to run their races on their own terms. Why it matters: Republican lawmakers fled Washington for the latter part of the summer, eager to localize their races. But President Trump keeps nationalizing the election. In the process, he's staking out positions that run counter to GOP orthodoxy on issues including beef imports and child care subsidies . Driving the news: The Trump administration's plan to extend federal child care subsidies to families with a stay-at-home parent is the latest policy flashpoint. His call to rename New Mexico is his most recent cultural one. The child care proposal — championed by Vice President Vance — sparked backlash from some conservative lawmakers and pundits who tagged the policy as "socialism" at a time when Republicans have made anti-socialism a central campaign message. And whatever the merits of calling New Mexico "New America," it's likely not what Greg Cunningham, the GOP candidate in NM-03, will focus on when he takes the stage at the convention. Between the lines: Although Trump isn't formally taking attendance at the convention, there will be some notable absences. Sen. Susan Collins won't make it — and isn't making an excuse. Sen. Dan Sullivan will stay home to prepare for a Saturday debate. More than 100 GOP lawmakers are expected to skip the event. Zoom out: Trump has repeatedly forced Republicans to grapple with policies that aggravate their constituencies or collide with their own ideological convictions. His plan to import up to 300,000 metric tons of beef tariff-free for 90 days inflamed GOP lawmakers in red states. More than a dozen GOP senators publicly criticized the move, warning it would hurt American cattle ranchers. Imposing higher tariffs on Canadian goods threatened to bring a trade war to two must-win border states: Maine and Michigan. And his call Monday to target Canadian…

33e1d7779a:866b302f532536f9.title: Historic NYT v. OpenAI copyright battle heats up
33e1d7779a:866b302f532536f9.author: Sara Fischer
33e1d7779a:866b302f532536f9.summary: A landmark copyright lawsuit filed by the New York Times against OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 moved into a critical new phase Friday, as all three parties presented their official arguments to a judge, with hopes of a favorable ruling ahead of a possible trial. Why it matters: A ruling in favor of the Times could wreak havoc on the lucrative business models underpinning the AI industry. A ruling in favor of OpenAI and Microsoft would serve as a massive blow to the publishing industry, potentially undermining its ability to control and monetize how content is scraped and used by AI giants. Zoom in: In its motion for summary judgment, the Times argued OpenAI and Microsoft copied its works at scale to build commercial substitutes, which it believes violates the law. OpenAI argued existing copyright laws and legal precedents allow tech giants to scrape publicly available works to train their large language models, and that reported facts are not protected by copyright law. It cited studies that suggest outputs to queries via ChatGPT do not create commercial substitutes of the Times' work. Microsoft made similar claims for its Copilot AI product. How it works: In its filing, OpenAI cites two recent California federal court decisions, Kadrey v. Meta and Bartz v. Anthropic, which found using copyrighted works to train AI models constituted as "fair use" in both of those cases because the training was considered transformative. The Times disputes that the AI training was transformative, and also says those cases are different and can't be applied to this suit because those plaintiffs didn't show that AI outputs competed with their products, creating market substitutions for their journalism. Peter Oberacker, is too flawed to seriously compete, sources tell Axios. Why it matters: Expect to see more of this cold calculus as the general election heats up, with both parties determining where their money will actually make enough of a difference to be worth spending. In this case, the GOP has determined that New York's 19th district, a perennial battleground seat that has routinely changed hands between Democrats and Republicans over the last several election cycles, doesn't warrant the investment. The seat, currently held by freshman Rep. Josh Riley (D-N.Y.), was one of the National Republican Congressional Committee's stated targets as recently as last month . Driving the news: Congressional Leadership Fund, House Republicans' main super PAC, removed all its money in the district last week, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact. The group had $4.8 million in television ad reservations supporting Oberacker, all of which were pulled on Friday. The NRCC also removed Oberacker from its "MAGA Majority" list, according to Punchbowl News . The NRCC and CLF did not provide comments on the record for this story. Between the lines: Oberacker is seen by Republicans on Capitol Hill as too flawed a candidate to seriously challenge Riley, according to multiple GOP sources familiar with the matter. One major issue that sources cited is the controversy around a post Oberacker made on Facebook in 2015 praising his grandfather's military service in Nazi Germany. Another is his campaign's cash burn rate: He had raised around $1.2 million as of the end of June but spent nearly $850,000 of it, including $350,000 on consultants, according to campaign finance filings. The Oberacker campaign's spending, one source told Axios, has been a source of behind-the-scenes tension with national Republicans. What we're hearing:…

Why it matters: It's an ignominious turn of events for a brash organization that lured some of the biggest stars away from the PGA Tour with enormous paydays that proved to be unsustainable. The big picture: LIV represents a high-profile flop for its Saudi investors. The bankruptcy filing comes after months of efforts to lure new backers and chart a new path for a league that struggled to draw significant TV ratings. Catch up quick: The Public Investment Fund — Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund — confirmed in April that it was withdrawing support for the league after the 2026 season. PIF — which ultimately plunged more than $5 billion into LIV, according to Money in Sport — decided to ditch LIV after President Trump's war in Iran scrambled geopolitics in the Middle East and jolted energy prices. The fund said in a statement that the "substantial investment required by LIV Golf over a longer term is no longer consistent with the current phase of PIF's investment strategy." Between the lines: LIV said Tuesday that it had secured a restructuring support agreement from an arm of BC Partners to reorganize operations and emerge "majority owned by players." The bankruptcy could lead to the severing of key contracts, including with star players like Jon Rahm, whose defection to LIV was considered a significant loss for the PGA Tour. It could also serve as a major turning point in the career of superstar Bryson DeChambeau, one of the initial players to leave the PGA for LIV. PGA Tour CEO Brian Rolapp has made it clear that any players who want to return will need to earn their way back, calling the tour a meritocracy by its nature. 33e1d7779a:73406160ff35370f.title: AI agents are poised to be the next hacking victims, cyber CEO predicts

33e1d7779a:73406160ff35370f.summary: In a world of AI-enabled cyberattacks , the victims of hacks will no longer just be humans — they'll also be AI agents themselves, Bugcrowd CEO Dave Gerry told Axios. Why it matters: Cyber defenses are tailored toward predicting and defending humans. Now, companies need to start treating the agents roaming their systems as both potential adversaries and the targets. Driving the news: Gerry's prediction during an interview at the Black Hat cybersecurity conference last month came after OpenAI disclosed that its agentic system hacked Hugging Face but before the AI lab released its technical deep dive into how its agents carried out that attack. What he's saying: "We're going to see agents as the victim," Gerry told Axios. "You're going to start to see agents getting hacked, not people." The big picture : Gerry's prediction comes as AI labs continue to grapple with the long-tail impact of their agents taking unauthorized actions during pre-deployment security testing. But many of those cases involve AI agents acting in unintended ways, not hacking each other as a way to break into an organization. Zoom in: Gerry fully anticipates that the growing number of hacks against AI agents are going to take place in the enterprise, rather than on consumer-owned and operated agents, since that's where the bulk of AI agents are currently deployed. "It's going to become the No. 1 attack vector that we're going to see," he said. "To make our lives easier as humans, we've given [AI agents] the crown jewels to everything." He noted that many tools that companies have long relied on now also have agents themselves, making it harder to keep track of what's on a company network. "You have all of these enterprise-approved tools that now magically got AI turned on," he said. "Now, there's a backlog of all of this tech debt of things that I approved that I no longer approve."
